extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of philosophy; seekers of a general method for reasoning and scientific inquiry
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for constructing a personal method to conduct one's reason and seek truth in the sciences, including explicit methodological precepts, provisional moral rules for action while epistemic work proceeds, and comments on the limits of existing arts (logic, algebra, analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept only clear and distinct truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Never to accept anything for true which I did not clearly know to be such; that is to say, carefully to avoid precipitancy and prejudice, and to comprise nothing more in my judgement than what was presented to my mind so clearly and distinctly as to exclude all ground of doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the primary epistemic rule: refuse assent to anything not felt as evident. The text warns against precipitancy and prejudice and treats clear and distinct perception as the criterion that excludes doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide problems into as many parts as necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: To divide each of the difficulties under examination into as many parts as possible, and as might be necessary for its adequate solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analysis: break complex problems into simpler subproblems so each can be handled more readily. The rule is presented as a formal precept of the method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order inquiry from simple to complex
rubrics_metrics.description: To conduct my thoughts in such order that, by commencing with objects the simplest and easiest to know, I might ascend by little and little, and, as it were, step by step, to the knowledge of the more complex; assigning in thought a certain order even to those objects which in their own nature do not stand in a relation of antecedence and sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with the most elementary truths and build upward. This guides selection and sequencing of premises and arguments; Descartes cites the mathematicians' success with chains of simple reasonings as a model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make complete enumerations and reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: In every case to make enumerations so complete, and reviews so general, that I might be assured that nothing was omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure comprehensiveness: when solving a problem, enumerate conditions and possibilities exhaustively to avoid overlooking elements that could invalidate conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mathematical abstraction and general relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider proportions in the most general form possible and represent them by the simplest objects (e.g., straight lines) or by brief characters so that relations can be applied across different domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrow strengths of geometry and algebra: represent relations abstractly and symbolically to simplify reasoning, retain aggregates via concise notation, and enable transfer of methods between domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspend and rebuild inherited opinions (methodic doubt)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve at once to sweep away all previously held opinions so as to be in a position to admit others more correct, or to scrutinize even the same when examined by reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A methodological skepticism: set aside received opinions (without rashness) to reconstruct beliefs on foundations one has personally verified using the method's rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a unified system guided by simple principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The example that works planned by a single master (architect, legislator) are more elegant/consistent than patchworks; thus seek a single guiding principle rather than a massing of disparate opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for coherence and unity in theory-building; avoid theories that are merely aggregations of many conflicting opinions without an organizing principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about relying on ordinary logic/syllogisms for discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic's syllogisms and many of its precepts are useful for communicating what we already know, but are limited for investigating the unknown; many logical precepts are injurious or superfluous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat traditional syllogistic logic as insufficient for discovery; instead prefer rules modeled on demonstrative chains (as in mathematics) and on analysis/symbolization where helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose moderate, locally practical opinions as provisional conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Obey the laws and customs of my country and regulate conduct according to the most moderate opinions adopted in practice by the most judicious among those with whom I live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a 'provisory' moral rule while epistemic reconstruction proceeds: adopt moderate, socially practicable beliefs for day-to-day action (especially those of the judicious in one's community) rather than extreme positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be resolute in action; act on the most probable when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Be as firm and resolute in my actions as possible, and not to adhere less steadfastly to the most doubtful opinions, when once adopted, than if they had been highly certain; when it is not possible to determine what is true, act according to what is most probable and thereafter treat it, in practice, as certain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practical decision-making under uncertainty: pick a course (even if only probably correct), then commit to it for action rather than remaining indecisive. This reduces remorse and paralysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceed slowly and with circumspection in intellectual reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceed so slowly and with such circumspection that, if I did not advance far, I would at least guard against falling; do not rashly reject all former beliefs without careful consideration of the task and proper preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intellectual reform should be cautious: carefully prepare (eradicate erroneous opinions, amass experience, practice the method) before tackling foundational principles to avoid getting lost or making premature errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer experience and practical testing over mere speculative ingenuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Find more truth in reasonings of individuals about affairs in which they are personally interested (and which have practical consequences) than in speculative scholastic exercises remote from practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value empirically tested judgments and experiences that have immediate consequences over purely speculative arguments; use experience as material for reasoned inquiry and for testing reconstructed principles.
